title: A / an, the and zero article 2

sections.title: Jobs and positions
sections.content:
We use a / an to talk about a type of job:
• She was a company director when she retired.
• Against her parents' wishes, she wants to be a journalist.
However, when we give a person's job title, or their unique position, we use the or zero article (i.e. no article), not a / an. Compare:
• She's been appointed (the) head of the company. and I'm a production manager at Fino. (= there may be more than one production manager)
After the position of, the post of, or the role of we use zero article before a job title:
• Dr Simons has taken on the position of Head of Department.

sections.title: Names of people
sections.content:
We usually use zero article before the name of an individual person or place. However, we use the:
- when there are two people with the same name to specify which one we mean:
• That's not the Stephen Fraser I went to school with. (but compare 'There was a Stephen Fraser in my class.' = a person named Stephen Fraser)
- when we want to emphasise that the person we are referring to is the most famous person with that name. Used this way, the is stressed and pronounced /ði:/:
• Do they mean the Neil Armstrong, or someone else?
- with an adjective to describe a person, or another noun which tells us their job:
• the late Stephen Hawking (= no longer alive)
• (the) artist Joseph Turner ('the' is sometimes left out, particularly in journalism)
- when we talk about a family as a whole:
• The Robinsons are away this weekend.

sections.title: Names as qualities or products
sections.content:
Note that a / an, or sometimes zero article, is used with a name when referring to the particular excellent qualities of the person named:
• Majid plays tennis well, but he'll never be (a) Roger Federer.
We also use a / an when we refer to an individual example of a product made by a particular manufacturer (e.g I've just bought a Mercedes) or a work by a particular artist (e.g. Do you think it could be a Van Gogh / a Rembrandt?).
You can use a / an before a person's name if you don't know the person yourself:
• Dr Lee is here for you. (= I know Dr Lee) and There's a Dr Amy Lee on the phone. (= I haven't heard of her before)

sections.title: This instead of a / an in stories
sections.content:
When telling stories and jokes, this is commonly used instead of a / an to introduce a new person or thing. Using this highlights the person or thing as the topic of what is to come next:
• As I was walking along, this spider (= a spider) landed on my head, and ...
• This man (= a man) goes into a chemist and he says ...

sections.title: Superlative adjectives
sections.content:
We use the before a superlative adjective (the biggest, the most expensive, etc.) when the superlative adjective is followed by a noun or defining phrase:
• He is the finest young player around at the moment.
However, we can often leave out the, particularly in an informal style, when there is no noun or defining phrase after the superlative adjective. Compare:
• It was (the) cheapest. and It was the cheapest I could find.

exercises.question: She was determined to be author one day. (Find the mistake).
exercises.hint: Use 'a/an' to talk about a type of job.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: be author -> be an author
Use 'a/an' to talk about a type of job. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.sentence: She was determined to be an author one day and worked hard towards her goal.
exercises.correction: She was determined to be an author one day and worked hard towards her goal.
acceptable: She was determined to be an author one day and worked hard towards her goal.
exercises.hint: 'An author' — use 'an' before a vowel sound. This is correct.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: an author — CORRECT
'Author' begins with the vowel sound /ɔː/, so 'an' is correct. This sentence is grammatically accurate. Note: use 'a' or 'an' (not 'the') for jobs and roles when referring to one person as a type: 'become an author', 'be a teacher', 'work as an engineer'.
exercises.prompt: Is this sentence correct? If not, rewrite it correctly.

exercises.question: I didn't even know Clara was interested in art until I heard that she owns Van Gogh.
options: owns Van Gogh -> owns a Van Gogh
I didn't even know -> I hadn't even known
exercises.hint: Use 'a' / 'an' for a work by a particular artist.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: owns Van Gogh -> owns a Van Gogh
Use 'a' / 'an' for a work by a particular artist. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.sentence: He is the best player in a team and everyone knows it.
exercises.correction: He is the best player in the team and everyone knows it.
exercises.hint: 'The team' — a specific, already-identified group takes 'the'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: the best player in the team
'The team' refers to a specific team already established in context. 'A team' would suggest an unspecified team. Also: superlatives ('the best', 'the most', 'the fastest') require 'the' because they point to a unique, identified entity.

exercises.question: I'm ___ marketing adviser at Dozzle.
exercises.hint: Use 'a' for a type of job.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: a
Use the indefinite article 'a/an' when describing someone's job or role: 'I'm a teacher', 'She's an engineer'. This is a general classification, not a specific individual.

exercises.question: She plays ___ violin in a professional orchestra. She started at age four.
exercises.hint: Musical instruments take 'the' when referring to playing them.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: the violin
When referring to playing a musical instrument as a skill or activity, use 'the': play the piano, play the violin, play the guitar. This is a fixed convention in standard British and American English. Exception: jazz musicians sometimes omit 'the' in informal contexts.

exercises.question: She has been appointed ___ Minister for Industry. (Give all possible answers).
exercises.hint: For a unique position/title, use 'the' or zero article.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: the / zero article
For a unique position/title, use 'the' or zero article. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: Rodrigo's boat wasn't the most elegant in the harbour, but it was certainly ___ biggest. Can we omit 'the'?
exercises.hint: When there is no noun or defining phrase after the superlative, 'the' can often be left out.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Yes (biggest)
When there is no noun or defining phrase after the superlative, 'the' can often be left out.
